blocks.text: A newborn baby cannot shiver effectively, yet it keeps its body temperature steady in a cool room. It does so with brown adipose tissue, whose mitochondria burn fuel at a high rate and release the energy as heat instead of ATP. The same mitochondrial machinery that normally makes ATP can be deliberately short-circuited. To see how, we must follow electrons from NADH to oxygen and see what the energy of that journey is spent on.

blocks.markdown: The reduced coenzymes NADH and FADH2, made by glycolysis, fatty acid oxidation and the citric acid cycle, are oxidised by the **electron transport chain (respiratory chain)** in the **inner mitochondrial membrane**. Electrons flow from carriers of low reduction potential (NADH) to carriers of higher potential and finally to **molecular oxygen**, the terminal acceptor, which is reduced to water. This flow is strongly exergonic. The energy is not released as heat in one step; it is used to pump protons across the inner membrane, and the resulting gradient is used to make ATP. This coupling of electron transport to ATP synthesis is **oxidative phosphorylation**.

blocks.title: Chemiosmotic coupling
blocks.text: In Mitchell's chemiosmotic theory, electron transport pumps protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space, creating a proton-motive force (a chemical gradient of H+ plus an electrical potential, negative inside the matrix). ATP synthase uses the energy released as protons flow back into the matrix through it to make ATP from ADP and inorganic phosphate.

rows: Cytochrome c to O2, forming H2O
blocks.caption: The four respiratory complexes. Ubiquinone (coenzyme Q) and cytochrome c are mobile carriers linking them. Proton numbers are those commonly quoted in textbooks.

blocks.markdown: **Electron flow.** NADH donates electrons to **Complex I**, which passes them to **ubiquinone (Q)** while pumping 4 H+. FADH2 enters differently: **Complex II** (the same enzyme as succinate dehydrogenase of the citric acid cycle) passes its electrons to Q **without pumping protons**. Reduced ubiquinone (ubiquinol) carries electrons to **Complex III**, which pumps 4 H+ and passes electrons to the small soluble protein **cytochrome c**. Cytochrome c carries them to **Complex IV**, which reduces O2 to H2O and pumps 2 H+. Therefore one NADH sends electrons through I, III and IV and pumps about 10 H+, whereas one FADH2 bypasses Complex I and pumps about 6 H+.

blocks.caption: Overall reaction of the respiratory chain for one NADH; the energy released drives proton pumping.

blocks.markdown: **ATP synthase (Complex V)** has two parts: **F0**, a proton channel in the inner membrane with a rotating ring of c-subunits, and **F1**, which protrudes into the matrix and contains the catalytic sites. Protons flowing down their gradient through F0 force the ring and central shaft to rotate; the rotation changes the conformation of the three catalytic subunits of F1 in turn, so that they bind ADP and phosphate, form ATP, and release it (the binding change mechanism). Roughly 4 H+ are needed per ATP, 3 to turn the c-ring and 1 to bring phosphate and exchange ATP for ADP across the membrane. The proton gradient therefore links the two halves of oxidative phosphorylation, and **respiratory control** means that electron transport slows when ADP is scarce because the gradient is not being used.

blocks.title: ATP yield of one NADH from proton counting
blocks.prompt: Taking 10 H+ pumped per NADH and 4 H+ consumed per ATP made, calculate the ATP produced per NADH.

steps.text: NADH feeds Complex I (4 H+), then Complex III (4 H+), then Complex IV (2 H+): total 4 + 4 + 2 = 10 H+.
Divide by the proton cost of making an ATP.

blocks.answer: About 2.5 ATP per NADH, the commonly used value (older texts say 3).

rows: Complex IV (bind its iron, preventing O2 reduction)
blocks.caption: Inhibitors and uncouplers of oxidative phosphorylation.

blocks.markdown: **Predicting effects.** *Inhibitors of the chain* (rotenone, antimycin A, cyanide) stop electron flow; proton pumping stops, the gradient collapses, ATP synthesis falls, NADH accumulates and the citric acid cycle slows; cells shift to anaerobic glycolysis and lactate rises. *Cyanide* is dangerous because it binds Complex IV, so oxygen cannot be used even when it is abundant; tissue oxygen consumption falls and venous blood stays oxygen-rich. *Uncouplers* make the inner membrane leaky to protons: the gradient is dissipated, so ATP synthesis falls, but electron transport runs faster because it is no longer limited by the gradient, so O2 consumption rises and the energy escapes as heat. **UCP1 (thermogenin)** of brown adipose tissue is a physiological uncoupler.

blocks.title: Predicting the response to an ATP synthase inhibitor
blocks.prompt: Isolated mitochondria are respiring on NADH-linked substrates with plenty of ADP and phosphate. Oligomycin, which blocks the F0 channel of ATP synthase, is added. Predict the changes in ATP synthesis, proton gradient and O2 consumption.

steps.text: Oligomycin blocks the proton channel of F0, so protons cannot re-enter through ATP synthase and ATP synthesis stops.
The complexes keep pumping protons for a short time, so the gradient builds up. A larger gradient makes the next proton harder to pump.
Electron transport is therefore slowed or stopped, so O2 consumption falls. This is respiratory control in action.

blocks.answer: ATP synthesis stops, the proton gradient increases, and O2 consumption falls.

items: Electron route: NADH to Complex I to Q to Complex III to cytochrome c to Complex IV to O2; succinate enters at Complex II.
Complexes I, III and IV pump protons; Complex II does not.
ATP synthase makes ATP as protons flow back through F0; about 4 H+ per ATP.
Cyanide blocks Complex IV; uncouplers allow protons to leak back so that ATP falls and heat rises.

blocks.title: Coupling and control
blocks.text: Electron transport and ATP synthesis are normally tightly coupled: neither proceeds quickly without the other. Inhibitors of electron flow and of ATP synthase both reduce O2 use; only an uncoupler increases O2 use while lowering ATP production.

points: Electrons flow from NADH through Complexes I, III and IV (FADH2 via Complex II) to O2; Complexes I, III and IV pump protons.
The proton-motive force drives ATP synthase (F0 channel, F1 catalytic head), roughly 4 H+ per ATP.
Cyanide blocks Complex IV and stops respiration; uncouplers dissipate the gradient, raising O2 consumption and heat while lowering ATP.

questions.stem: Which molecule is the final electron acceptor of the mitochondrial respiratory chain, and at which complex is it reduced?

options.text: Oxygen, at Complex IV
NAD+, at Complex I
Ubiquinone, at Complex II
Cytochrome c, at Complex III

distractorRationale.a: Correct: cytochrome c oxidase reduces O2 to water.
distractorRationale.b: NAD+ is the oxidised form of the electron donor, not the final acceptor.
distractorRationale.c: Ubiquinone is a mobile intermediate carrier.
distractorRationale.d: Cytochrome c is an intermediate carrier between Complexes III and IV.

questions.explanation: Electrons are passed from NADH through carriers of rising reduction potential to Complex IV, where they reduce molecular oxygen to water. Ubiquinone and cytochrome c are intermediates.

questions.stem: A student is asked which respiratory complex receives electrons from succinate but does not pump protons. Which should she name?

options.text: Complex II
Complex I
Complex III
Complex IV

distractorRationale.a: Correct: succinate dehydrogenase passes electrons to ubiquinone without pumping protons.
distractorRationale.b: Complex I accepts electrons from NADH and pumps 4 H+.
distractorRationale.c: Complex III pumps 4 H+ and does not directly oxidise succinate.
distractorRationale.d: Complex IV reduces oxygen and pumps protons.

questions.explanation: Complex II is succinate dehydrogenase, shared with the citric acid cycle. It feeds electrons to ubiquinone but releases too little energy to pump protons, which is why FADH2 yields fewer ATP than NADH.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes how the proton gradient drives ATP synthesis?

options.text: Protons flow from the intermembrane space to the matrix through F0, rotating the shaft so that F1 forms ATP
Protons flow from the matrix to the intermembrane space through F1, directly phosphorylating ADP
The gradient transfers a phosphate group from creatine phosphate to ADP
Protons are pumped by ATP synthase using the energy of NADH

questions.correctOptionText: Protons flow from the intermembrane space to the matrix through F0, rotating the shaft so that F1 forms ATP

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the flow through F0 drives rotation and conformational changes in F1.
distractorRationale.b: The direction is the reverse, and the proton channel is F0, not F1.
distractorRationale.c: Creatine phosphate is a separate phosphate store and is unrelated.
distractorRationale.d: Complexes I, III and IV pump protons; ATP synthase uses their flow.

questions.explanation: The respiratory complexes pump protons into the intermembrane space, creating a gradient. Protons flowing back into the matrix through the F0 channel rotate the c-ring and shaft, and this rotation drives ATP formation in the F1 catalytic head.

questions.stem: A firefighter is rescued from a burning building and has a very high blood lactate, yet his venous blood oxygen saturation is high. Cyanide from burning plastics is suspected. Which mechanism best explains the findings?

options.text: Cyanide blocks Complex IV, so tissues cannot use oxygen, ATP falls and cells shift to anaerobic glycolysis
Cyanide uncouples the membrane so oxygen use rises and the tissues become hypoxic
Cyanide inhibits ATP synthase so that the proton gradient rises and oxygen use increases
Cyanide inhibits Complex I selectively, sparing FADH2-linked oxidation

questions.correctOptionText: Cyanide blocks Complex IV, so tissues cannot use oxygen, ATP falls and cells shift to anaerobic glycolysis

distractorRationale.a: Correct: oxygen is delivered but not consumed, so venous saturation stays high while lactate rises.
distractorRationale.b: Uncouplers increase oxygen use; cyanide reduces it.
distractorRationale.c: Inhibition of ATP synthase raises the gradient but reduces, not increases, O2 consumption, and is not the action of cyanide.
distractorRationale.d: Cyanide acts at Complex IV, which all electron routes share.

questions.explanation: Cyanide binds the iron of cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV), so no electron route can reach oxygen. Oxygen therefore remains in venous blood, ATP production falls, NADH accumulates and cells rely on glycolysis, producing lactate.

questions.stem: A patient who took an illicit weight-loss compound containing 2,4-dinitrophenol presents with fever and sweating. Which pattern of changes is expected in her mitochondria?

options.text: Increased oxygen consumption, decreased ATP synthesis and increased heat production
Decreased oxygen consumption, decreased ATP synthesis and decreased heat
Increased ATP synthesis with a larger proton gradient
Decreased oxygen consumption with a larger proton gradient

questions.correctOptionText: Increased oxygen consumption, decreased ATP synthesis and increased heat production

distractorRationale.a: Correct: an uncoupler dissipates the gradient, so electron transport speeds up without ATP production.
distractorRationale.b: This would fit an inhibitor of the chain, not an uncoupler.
distractorRationale.c: An uncoupler collapses the gradient and reduces ATP synthesis.
distractorRationale.d: This resembles the effect of an ATP synthase inhibitor, not an uncoupler.

questions.explanation: 2,4-Dinitrophenol carries protons across the inner membrane, dissipating the gradient. Without back-pressure from the gradient, electron transport and O2 consumption accelerate, yet ATP synthesis falls and the energy is released as heat, producing fever.

questions.stem: Oligomycin blocks the proton channel of ATP synthase. In actively respiring isolated mitochondria with ample ADP, what happens to oxygen consumption, and why?

options.text: It falls, because protons accumulate in the intermembrane space and the gradient opposes further pumping
It rises, because the blocked enzyme releases extra electrons
It is unchanged, because electron transport is independent of ATP synthase
It falls, because oligomycin directly binds Complex IV

questions.correctOptionText: It falls, because protons accumulate in the intermembrane space and the gradient opposes further pumping

distractorRationale.a: Correct: coupling means the gradient must be used for electron transport to continue at a high rate.
distractorRationale.b: Blocking the channel does not release electrons.
distractorRationale.c: Electron transport is coupled to the gradient, so it is not independent.
distractorRationale.d: Oligomycin acts on F0, not on Complex IV.

questions.explanation: With the F0 channel blocked, protons cannot flow back and the gradient rises, making further proton pumping harder. Electron transport and O2 consumption therefore fall, an example of respiratory control.

questions.stem: True or false: oxidation of FADH2 via Complex II yields less ATP than oxidation of NADH because electrons from FADH2 bypass Complex I, which pumps protons.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Electrons from FADH2 enter at Complex II, which does not pump protons, so fewer protons (about 6) are pumped than for NADH (about 10). Fewer protons means less ATP, about 1.5 compared with 2.5.

questions.stem: Isolated mitochondria oxidise succinate, passing electrons through Complexes II, III and IV. Complex II pumps no protons, Complex III pumps 4 H+ and Complex IV pumps 2 H+ per pair of electrons. If ATP synthase requires 4 H+ per ATP, calculate the ATP yield per succinate oxidised.
questions.explanation: Protons pumped per succinate are 0 + 4 + 2 = 6 H+. Dividing by 4 H+ per ATP gives 6 / 4 = 1.5 ATP. This is why FADH2-linked substrates give fewer ATP than NADH-linked ones, which yield 10 / 4 = 2.5.

questions.stem: Outline the flow of electrons from NADH and from succinate to oxygen through the respiratory chain, indicate where protons are pumped, and explain how the resulting gradient drives ATP synthesis.
markingGuide: NADH to Complex I to ubiquinone (Q) to Complex III to cytochrome c to Complex IV to O2 (forming water)
Succinate (FADH2) enters at Complex II, which passes electrons to Q and does not pump protons
Protons are pumped into the intermembrane space at Complexes I, III and IV
Proton gradient (proton-motive force) across the inner membrane forms; matrix negative and alkaline
Protons return through F0 of ATP synthase, rotating the c-ring and shaft; F1 binds ADP and Pi and forms ATP (binding change)
Approximately 2.5 ATP per NADH and 1.5 per FADH2 (about 4 H+ per ATP)
questions.explanation: Electrons move down a gradient of reduction potential, and the released energy is used to pump protons. The resulting proton-motive force drives ATP synthase, so electron transport is chemiosmotically coupled to ATP formation.

questions.stem: Compare the effects of cyanide poisoning and of an uncoupling agent on oxygen consumption, ATP synthesis, the proton gradient and heat production in a muscle cell.
markingGuide: Cyanide binds Complex IV, blocking electron transfer to O2; oxygen consumption falls
With cyanide, proton pumping stops, the gradient collapses and ATP synthesis falls; NADH accumulates, citric acid cycle slows and glycolysis and lactate increase
Uncoupler lets protons leak across the inner membrane, dissipating the gradient
With an uncoupler, electron transport is not limited by the gradient so oxygen consumption rises while ATP synthesis falls
Energy is released as heat with an uncoupler (fever, as with UCP1 in brown fat); no increase in heat with cyanide
Both lower ATP; the difference is the direction of change in O2 consumption
questions.explanation: Both agents lower ATP production, but by different mechanisms. Cyanide stops electron flow so oxygen use falls; an uncoupler removes the gradient so the chain runs faster, consumes more oxygen and releases the energy as heat.
